newsitem.title: USA: Clinton expands family leave for federal workers.
newsitem.headline: Clinton expands family leave for federal workers.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Saturday expanded family and medical leave for federal employees and urged Congress to extend similar rights to private sector workers.

Without waiting for lawmakers to act on his proposed legislation, Clinton used his executive powers to allow those who work for the federal government an extra 24 hours of leave without pay each year for school conferences and family members' doctor or dentist appointments.

"I think this bill is so important that today I am asking all federal departments and agencies to make expanded family and medical leave available to their workers immediately," he said in his weekly radio address.
"I want workers to have access right now to essential time off for family obligations," he added.
Clinton also called on Congress to do its part to come to the aid of American families.
"Don't ask people to choose ever between being good workers and good parents. We can help them to do both. Pass the expanded Family and Medical Leave Act," he said.
The legislation would allow all workers up to 24 hours of unpaid leave each year to fulfill family obligations such as routine medical or dental visits for their children or elderly relatives.
"It could allow a worker to attend a parent-teacher conference, or take a child to the pediatrician, or to find quality child care, or to care for an elderly relative," Clinton explained.

The current law, which Clinton pushed through Congress in 1993, permits workers to take up to 12 weeks unpaid leave to care for a newborn or adopted child, to attend to their own serious health needs, or to care for a seriously ill parent, child, or spouse.

The chairman for the House Education and the Workforce Committee questioned the timing and process by which Clinton would expand family leave, citing the rush to expand a law when "we're not sure it's working as originally intended."

"American workers ... would be better served if we slowed the process just a little, carefully examined the FMLA and then made improvements to the law as needed," said Bill Goodling, a Pennsylvania Republican.
Last June, Clinton proposed expanding the measure to include 24 hours of unpaid leave to accommodate other family and medical circumstances.

In his radio address, Clinton also said he and wife Hillary Rodham Clinton would bring together researchers, parents and other experts for a White House Conference on Early Childhood Development and Learning next week.
The meeting, which will focus on what new research on the brain has revealed about very early childhood, will be broadcast by satellite hookup to more than 60 sites around the country.

"From our research, we know that from the very first days of life a child is developing emotionally and intellectually, and how he or she does in those first three years of life will help to determine how a child does later in school and in life," Clinton said.
The president noted that Mrs. Clinton, in her best-selling book about child-rearing "It Takes a Village," recommended more attention be paid to new findings about the early years of childhood.
He said the conference would serve as a call to action to parents, businesses, care-givers, the media, the religious community and the government.
